content: 1. Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) has been shown to have a beneficial effect in reducing symptom severity in adults with PTSD. This effect has been demonstrated using both clinician-rated and patient-rated outcome measures. However, the confidence in this estimate is low, and it remains uncertain whether the effect persists at follow-up assessments due to the lack of systematic evidence. 2. Individual Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) with a trauma focus has demonstrated a beneficial effect in reducing PTSD symptom severity in adults. This effect has been observed through both clinician-rated and service user-rated outcome measures. The confidence in this estimate is moderate, and the effect appears to persist at follow-up assessments, although the confidence in follow-up estimates is low. 3. Group CBT with a trauma focus has also shown evidence of reducing PTSD symptom severity in adults. However, this effect has only been demonstrated using patient-rated outcome measures, and the confidence in this estimate is moderate. The persistence of the effect at follow-up assessments is uncertain, with low confidence in follow-up estimates. 4. Stress management interventions in adults with PTSD have shown evidence of reducing symptom severity post-intervention. This effect has been demonstrated using clinician-rated outcome measures only, and the confidence in this estimate is low. It is unclear whether the effect persists at follow-up assessments due to insufficient evidence. 5. Prolonged exposure therapy, a form of CBT, involves extensive exposure to distressing or traumatic memories. While effective, it can be counterintuitive and difficult for some individuals to endure. Despite this, research on exposure-based therapies for anxiety disorders consistently shows large effect sizes for symptom reduction. 6. EMDR does not require individuals to verbalize detailed accounts of their traumatic experiences, which may be advantageous in cases where discussing the trauma is particularly distressing or stigmatized. However, the underlying mechanisms of EMDR remain speculative, and this has been a source of controversy. 7. Stress management training can be implemented relatively easily and practiced in group settings by para-professionals. It has demonstrated value across a range of disorders and may be a feasible option in resource-constrained settings. 8. Most studies supporting the efficacy of CBT with a trauma focus and EMDR have been conducted in high-income countries by trained clinicians. Implementing these therapies in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) would require substantial resources, including additional training and supervision for clinicians. 9. The feasibility of implementing EMDR by non-specialized health staff remains uncertain, as there is no randomized evidence supporting its use in such settings. The EMDR Institute requires trainees to have a master’s degree or higher in the mental health field and to be licensed or certified for independent practice. 10. Psychological treatments based on CBT principles, including stress management and trauma-focused CBT, may help individuals develop long-term skills to address stressors and improve functioning. These skills can also be applied to the treatment of other disorders. 11. For children and adolescents with PTSD, psychological interventions such as individual and group CBT with a trauma focus, EMDR, and stress management have been evaluated. These interventions aim to reduce symptom severity, improve functioning and quality of life, and address the presence of mental disorders at follow-up. 12. Traditional CBT for PTSD involves teaching individuals skills to modify unhelpful thoughts and behaviors, leading to improved emotional well-being. In contrast, EMDR does not involve direct targeting of beliefs or behaviors, does not require daily homework, and does not necessitate detailed recounting of the traumatic event. 13. The theoretical mechanisms underlying EMDR remain largely speculative, which has contributed to ongoing debate about its efficacy and implementation. 14. Psychological interventions for PTSD in children and adolescents have been systematically reviewed, focusing on individual and group CBT, EMDR, and stress management. These reviews assess outcomes such as symptom severity, functioning, quality of life, and adverse effects. 15. The implementation of psychological interventions in LMICs may face challenges due to limited training and resources among primary healthcare staff. Additional training in CBT with a trauma focus and EMDR would require significant investment in supervision and capacity building. 16. In resource-constrained settings, stress management may be the most feasible treatment option despite evidence suggesting that individual CBT with a trauma focus is more effective. 17. Bereavement interventions, such as benzodiazepines, have been evaluated for their efficacy in adults, but their use in PTSD treatment remains limited and context-dependent.
